metadata.file_name: 51. Jewsbury et al. (2025). Irt‑latent regression with many predictors: limits and solutions.pdf
metadata.title: Irt‑latent regression with many predictors: limits and solutions

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper does not analyze an operational ILSA micro-dataset with a complex sampling design; instead, it uses simulation data generated for N=1000 test takers per simulated assessment across 1000 replications per condition. Because there is no survey sampling, no stratification/clustering, and no ILSA sampling weights are defined or applied, student/sampling weights are not part of the estimation procedure. The PV generation and regression estimation are performed within the simulation framework using fixed item parameters and marginal-maximum likelihood (EM) for the latent regression coefficients. As a result, weighting guidance for real ILSA data is conceptual: in operational settings, PVs are typically generated under the IRT-latent regression model and then combined using multiple-imputation rules, but this paper’s instability findings are driven by the interaction of predictor dimensionality, test information (items per person), and missingness—not by survey weights.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Simulation study: for each of 1000 simulated assessments per condition, the authors generated data for N=1000 test takers. Each test taker received item responses from a pool of 40 dichotomous items (3PL or 2PL), with the number of observed item responses J determined by the assessment design condition (e.g., J=4/6/8/12) and missingness introduced under MCAR (No missing: all test takers have J observed responses; Missing: 70% have J observed responses and 10% each have 1, 2, and 3 observed responses). No real-country sampling frame or analytic filtering from an operational ILSA dataset is used.

main_findings.dataset_used: Simulation study of IRT-latent regression with PVs (N=1000 test takers; 40 items; 2PL/3PL; PVs M=20)
main_findings.target_variable: Population mean and distribution moments of latent proficiency (PV-based estimators)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bias patterns reported in Tables 1 and 3–6: as P increases, bias for population mean/skewness becomes increasingly negative in difficult 3PL; variance and kurtosis bias increases; extreme percentiles (10th/90th) show stronger outward bias than median. Example magnitude: in difficult 3PL with Missing and J=4, mean population variance estimate exceeds true variance by 52.7%; in moderate 2PL with No missing and J=4, variance overestimation is 2.4%.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data for IRT-latent regression with PVs, the study leveraged number of predictors (P), items per test taker (J), item missingness condition, and IRT item model type to estimate population moments and percentiles of latent proficiency, finding that estimator bias grows with P particularly when measurement precision is low for a substantial share of test takers (e.g., difficult 3PL and Missing). This indicates that expanding the predictor set in large-scale assessments can undermine validity unless assessment designs ensure at least moderate measurement precision for all test takers, especially for low-proficiency groups.

main_findings.dataset_used: Simulation study of IRT-latent regression with PVs (N=1000 test takers; 40 items; 3PL/2PL; PVs M=20)
main_findings.target_variable: Group mean and group variance of latent proficiency (PV-based estimators)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Bias patterns reported in Tables 2 and 4–6: as P increases, group mean estimates become more outwardly biased (G1 more negative, G5 more positive), and group variance biases increase most for extreme groups (G1 and G5). The rate of bias increase is larger for fewer items per test taker (low J) and larger under Missing (where 30% of test takers have only 1–3 observed items).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data for IRT-latent regression with PVs, the study leveraged number of predictors (P), items per test taker (J), item missingness condition, and IRT item model type to estimate group-level latent proficiency means and variances, finding that bias increases asymmetrically across ability groups as P grows, with the largest distortions for the lowest and highest proficiency groups under low-information designs. This indicates that policy-relevant subgroup reporting in large-scale assessments may become unstable when predictor dimensionality is increased without ensuring adequate test information across the full proficiency range.

main_findings.dataset_used: Simulation study of IRT-latent regression with PVs (PVs M=20; PVs generated conditional on fixed ML regression parameters vs sampled regression parameters)
main_findings.target_variable: Variance estimation consistency: PV-based vs plug-in estimators
main_findings.performance_metrics: Appendix C/D and Tables 7–11: plug-in and PV-based estimators are approximately equivalent for means and variances when PVs are generated conditional on fixed maximum-likelihood regression parameters; however, PV-based variance estimators using the operational procedure (PVs generated conditional on sampled regression parameters) produce additional positive bias relative to plug-in variance estimators, increasing with P.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using simulation data for IRT-latent regression with PVs, the study leveraged number of predictors (P) and assessment design conditions (J and missingness) to compare PV-based and plug-in variance estimation, finding that PV-based variance estimates become more positively biased when PVs are generated conditional on sampled regression parameters rather than fixed ML estimates. This indicates that operational PV-generation procedures can systematically inflate uncertainty estimates when predictor dimensionality is high, so variance reporting should be interpreted with design-aware caution.

data.outcome_summary: This paper is a simulation-based methodological study of the conventional large-scale assessment pipeline that models latent proficiency with IRT and then uses an IRT-latent regression to generate plausible values (PVs) for contextual inference. The authors simulate N=1000 test takers per assessment, generate item responses from 2PL or 3PL models, and vary assessment design conditions via the number of observed items per person (J) and an MCAR missingness mechanism (No missing vs Missing where 30% of test takers have only 1–3 observed items). They estimate IRT-latent regression models with increasing predictor dimensionality (P) using marginal maximum likelihood (EM) and generate M=20 PVs per test taker. Across conditions, bias in population and group moments grows with P, especially for difficult 3PL and Missing designs, while moderate 2PL designs with adequate information for all test takers remain robust even at low J. The study also shows that PV-based variance estimation depends on how PVs are generated (fixed ML vs sampled regression parameters), with operational sampling leading to additional positive variance bias that increases with P. Limitations: results are derived from controlled simulations with fixed item parameters and do not directly quantify performance on real operational ILSA datasets.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models (no supervised learners such as Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM are used). Instead, it develops and tests statistical properties of IRT-latent regression and PV-based estimators via simulation and theoretical derivations. Therefore, ml_techniques are intentionally empty and the study is classified as exploratory (methodological/simulation investigation rather than predictive ML).
